---
title: "Install & configure"
---

OMERO-Screen needs three things: the software, a configuration that names your
OMERO server and user, and your password. One command installs the software
and walks you through the rest. Budget ten minutes the first time, most of it
downloading.

## Which install do you need?

| You want to… | Use |
|---|---|
| analyse your plates on a Mac or Linux machine | [Quick install](#quick-install-macos-and-linux) |
| do the same on Windows | [Windows (WSL2)](#windows) |
| run jobs on an HPC cluster | [On an HPC cluster](#on-an-hpc-cluster) |
| try OMERO-Screen without an OMERO account | [Try it locally](try-it.qmd), with a local OMERO server in Docker |
| change the code | [Developer install](#developer-install) |

## Quick install (macOS and Linux)

Open **Terminal** and paste:

```bash
curl -LsSf https://raw.githubusercontent.com/HocheggerLab/omero-screen/main/install.sh | sh
```

The installer:

1. installs [uv](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/), which brings its own Python, if
   it is missing;
2. downloads the latest release and installs exactly the tested versions of
   everything, including napari, CellView, cellclass and the plotting
   library, into `~/.local/share/omero-screen`;
3. puts the commands (`omero-screen`, `cellview`, `cellclass`, `napari`, …) in
   uv's command directory (normally `~/.local/bin`) and adds that directory to
   your shell `PATH` automatically if needed;
4. downloads the stock Cellpose segmentation models, so a network problem
   shows up now rather than in the middle of your first plate;
5. runs `omero-screen setup` and `omero-screen doctor` (below).

If the installer says it updated your `PATH`, open a new Terminal window once
before running the commands. You do not need to edit `.zshrc` or another shell
file manually.

If the download fails (`could not download …`), check the network (VPN,
proxy) and run the same line again; it picks up where it stopped.

### Installer options

Set these as environment variables before `sh`, for example
`curl … | OMERO_SCREEN_NO_SETUP=1 sh`:

| Variable | Effect |
|---|---|
| `OMERO_SCREEN_VERSION` | install this release tag (e.g. `omero-screen-v0.10.4`) instead of the latest |
| `OMERO_SCREEN_HOME` | install here instead of `~/.local/share/omero-screen` (e.g. a project space with more room) |
| `OMERO_SCREEN_BIN` | link the commands here instead of uv's command directory; your `PATH` is then not changed |
| `OMERO_SCREEN_NO_SETUP=1` | skip `omero-screen setup` and `doctor` at the end |
| `OMERO_SCREEN_BRANCH` | install a branch instead of a release (for testing changes) |

### What goes where

| What | Where | Size |
|---|---|---|
| The software: one folder per release, each with its own Python environment | `~/.local/share/omero-screen/<release>`, with `current` pointing at the one in use | ~2.3 GB per release, two kept |
| The commands | `~/.local/bin` (links into `current`) | — |
| Your settings | `~/.config/omero-screen/config.toml` | — |
| Your password | the system keychain (or a password file, see below) | — |
| Cellpose models | `~/.cellpose/models` | 25 MB per Cellpose 3 model; 1.2 GB for Cellpose 4 (`cpsam`) |
| Downloaded images | `~/omero-cache` | grows with use |
| CellView database | `~/.cellview/cellview.duckdb` | grows with use |
| Downloaded packages, reused by updates | uv's cache (`uv cache dir`) | shared by all releases |

The two releases on disk share most of their files with uv's cache, so they
take less space than `du` reports, as long as the cache is on the same disk.

### Windows {#windows}

The installer is a shell script, and the local OMERO server needs Docker, which
on Windows runs on WSL2 anyway, so on Windows OMERO-Screen runs inside WSL2
(a Linux system built into Windows):

1. In PowerShell, run `wsl --install`, restart, and create a Linux user when
   Ubuntu opens.
2. In the Ubuntu window, run the [quick install](#quick-install-macos-and-linux)
   line.
3. For [Try it locally](try-it.qmd), install
   [Docker Desktop](https://docs.docker.com/desktop/setup/install/windows-install/)
   and turn on *Settings → Resources → WSL integration* for Ubuntu.

napari opens as a normal window on Windows 11. Without a keychain in WSL, use
a [password file](#the-configuration-in-detail).

::: {.callout-note}
The Windows route has not yet been tested end to end. Please report problems
as a GitHub issue.
:::

::: {.callout-note}
If you work with Claude, continue with [Working with Claude](claude.qmd) once
the installer has finished.
:::

## Update

```bash
omero-screen self update            # install the latest release
omero-screen self update --check    # only say whether there is one
```

Your settings and data are kept. `omero-screen doctor` also tells you when a
newer release is out. Running the install line again does the same as
`self update`.

The previous release stays on disk, so you can go back if a new one causes
trouble; older releases are removed (each takes several GB):

```bash
omero-screen self update --version 0.8.27
```

## Uninstall

```bash
omero-screen self uninstall           # remove the software and its commands
omero-screen self uninstall --purge   # also your settings and keychain password
```

What each operation does with the things listed in
[What goes where](#what-goes-where):

| | Update | Uninstall | Uninstall `--purge` |
|---|---|---|---|
| Software (current release) | replaced by the new one | removed | removed |
| Previous release | kept for rollback; older ones removed | removed | removed |
| Commands in `~/.local/bin` | relinked | removed (only ours) | removed (only ours) |
| Settings (`config.toml`) | kept | kept | **removed** |
| Keychain password | kept | kept | **removed** |
| Cellpose models, image cache, CellView database | kept | kept, listed | kept, listed |
| uv and its cache | kept | kept | kept |

Only commands that link into the install are removed; a `napari` you
installed yourself stays. Your data (the CellView database, the image cache
and the Cellpose models) is never deleted, not even with `--purge`: the
uninstaller lists where it is so you can delete it yourself.
`uv self uninstall` removes uv.

If the `omero-screen` command no longer works, uninstall from the web:

```bash
curl -LsSf https://raw.githubusercontent.com/HocheggerLab/omero-screen/main/install.sh | sh -s -- --uninstall
```

## Set up your OMERO login

```bash
omero-screen setup
```

It asks for:

- the **site profile**: a ready-made description of your server and
  microscopes. Choose `sussex` for the Hochegger lab OMERO, or `none` to type
  in a server name;
- your **OMERO user name** and **password**. The password is checked against
  the server, then stored in your computer's keychain (macOS Keychain), never
  in a file.

Your answers are saved in `~/.config/omero-screen/config.toml`. Run `setup`
again at any time to change them.

## Check the installation

```bash
omero-screen doctor
```

`doctor` checks everything OMERO-Screen needs (the software, your login, the
connection to the server, CellView, napari, the GPU and disk space) and says
how to fix anything that fails. If something does not work, run it first. A
failed connection is usually the VPN.

```bash
omero-screen config show      # the settings in effect, and where each came from
omero-screen --version        # the installed version
```

## Hardware

Segmentation and tracking are the expensive steps. Everything runs on a
laptop; some combinations need the right hardware.

| | Apple silicon (MPS) | NVIDIA (CUDA) | CPU only |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Default segmentation** | stock Cellpose 3 models (`nuclei`, `cyto3`) | Cellpose 4 (`cpsam`) | stock Cellpose 3, slow |
| **Cellpose 4** (`--cp4`) | not in practice: too slow and too large | yes | impractical |
| **Tracking** (`--track`) | falls back to CPU | yes | slow |
| **Classifier inference** | yes | yes | workable |

- **Segmentation models.** With no models configured, OMERO-Screen picks the
  best default for the machine and says so in the log. The stock Cellpose 3
  models segment most cells reasonably; a model trained on your own cells and
  microscope does better: see [Make a model for your cells](models.qmd).
- **The models used are recorded on every plate.** Each run writes the
  version, settings, device and models onto the plate in OMERO, so you can
  always tell how a plate was segmented.
- **Tracking has no MPS backend.** On Apple silicon, `--track` runs on the
  CPU: correct, but slow.

Device selection is automatic: CUDA if present, then MPS, then CPU. Force CPU
with `OMERO_SCREEN_USE_GPU=0`.

## On an HPC cluster

Run the [quick install](#quick-install-macos-and-linux) on a **login node**.
Then:

- **Password:** clusters have no keychain, so use a
  [password file](#the-configuration-in-detail).
- **Space:** each release takes ~2.3 GB. If your home directory is small, set
  `OMERO_SCREEN_HOME` (and `UV_CACHE_DIR`, uv's download cache) to a project
  directory.
- **Models:** fetch them on the login node once, so jobs don't download them
  in parallel: `omero-screen models pull stock`, and
  `omero-screen models pull hocheggerlab` for the lab's models. Cellpose 4
  (`cpsam`) downloads on first use.
- **CUDA:** the PyTorch build installed needs an NVIDIA driver for CUDA 12
  (driver 525 or newer).

The quick install includes napari, which needs glibc 2.34 or newer on Linux
(`ldd --version`). A GUI-free install for clusters, and an
`omero-screen submit` command that writes and submits SLURM jobs from the
install, are in preparation
([#92](https://github.com/HocheggerLab/omero-screen/issues/92)). Until then,
jobs are submitted from a source checkout as described in
[Running on a SLURM cluster](hpc.qmd).

## The configuration in detail

Settings come from several places. A value set higher up in this list wins:

1. command-line flags (e.g. `--cp4`);
2. environment variables (`HOST`, `USERNAME`, `OMERO_SCREEN_*`);
3. a `.env` file in a source checkout (developers, see below);
4. your **user config**, `~/.config/omero-screen/config.toml`;
5. the **site profile** it names;
6. built-in defaults.

A user config written by `setup` looks like this:

```toml
site = "sussex"

[omero]
username = "ab123"
# group = "my-lab-group"          # default: your OMERO default group

[segmentation]
# model_set = "hocheggerlab"      # the lab's models; first: omero-screen models pull hocheggerlab

[paths]
# cache = "~/omero-cache"         # downloaded images
# cellview_db = "~/.cellview/cellview.duckdb"

[env]
# any OMERO_SCREEN_* variable, e.g.
# OMERO_SCREEN_USE_GPU = "0"
```

A **site profile** holds what everyone at a site shares: the OMERO server and
port, the stitch calibrations of its microscopes, its model sets. `sussex` is
built in. For another site, write one as a TOML file, set
`site = "/path/to/your-site.toml"`, and send it to us so it can be included.

On a machine without a keychain (an HPC cluster), put the password in a file
only you can read and name it in the user config:

```bash
umask 077 && echo 'your-password' > ~/.omero-password
```

```toml
[omero]
password_file = "~/.omero-password"
```

The `PASSWORD` environment variable works too, and takes precedence.

## Working in another user's screens

To analyse plates that belong to someone else, you need at least read access
to their OMERO group. Your OMERO administrator sets this. Masks and results
are written to your own `Screens` project.

## Developer install

To work on the code, clone the repository and install the workspace with the
development tools:

```bash
git clone https://github.com/HocheggerLab/omero-screen.git
cd omero-screen
uv sync --dev
uv run omero-screen doctor
```

`uv sync` installs all six packages (the core pipeline, `cellview`,
`omero-screen-plots`, `omero-screen-napari`, `cellclass` and `omero-utils`).
Configure with `uv run omero-screen setup` as above. A `.env.development` (or
`.env.production`, selected with `ENV=production`) at the repository root is
still read and takes precedence over the user config:

```bash
USERNAME="your-omero-login"
PASSWORD="your-omero-password"
HOST="omero.your-institution.ac.uk"
```

::: {.callout-warning}
`.env.*` files hold your password in plain text. They are gitignored; keep it
that way, and never paste one into an issue or a pull request.
:::

Run `uv run omero-integration-test e2e_connection` to check the connection to
a test server.

### A release and a checkout side by side

You can keep the installed release for day-to-day work and a checkout for
development. They use separate Python environments: inside the checkout,
`uv run omero-screen` (or the checkout's activated `.venv`) runs your
development code; elsewhere, `omero-screen` runs the release. Check which one
you have with `omero-screen --version`.

They share your settings, keychain password, Cellpose models, image cache and
CellView database. Two things to watch:

- **`.env` files.** Any `omero-screen` command reads the `.env.{ENV}` file
  (default `.env.development`) of the git repository containing the current
  folder. Run inside your checkout, the release therefore uses the checkout's
  development settings. Run the release from outside any repository with a
  `.env` file.
- **Shared data.** Point the checkout at its own CellView database
  (`DATABASE_PATH` in `.env.development`) so experiments don't touch the one
  you work with.
